regional_origin: Tamil Sri Lanka (Northern and Eastern provinces)

ingredients.name: Urad dal (split white/black lentils)
ingredients.notes: about 1 cup; soaked in cold water for at least 4-6 hours (or overnight) before grinding

ingredients.name: Onion or shallots
ingredients.notes: finely chopped; do not add too much or the batter will become wet and soft

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.notes: to taste; add just before frying, not to the soaked dal

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: added gradually while grinding, just enough to make a smooth thick batter -- use as little as possible

ingredients.name: Oil for deep frying
ingredients.notes: enough to deep-fry; vegetable oil works, coconut oil gives extra flavour

steps.instruction: Wash the urad dal thoroughly in several changes of water, then soak in cold water for at least 4-6 hours, or overnight. The dal should double in size and become very soft.

Drain the soaked dal completely, shaking off as much water as possible. Transfer to a blender or wet grinder. Grind to a smooth, thick, fluffy batter, adding water only one tablespoon at a time -- use as little as possible. The batter is ready when it is light, airy, and holds its shape when a spoonful is dropped onto a wet palm.
Transfer the ground batter to a bowl. Add the chopped onion, green chillies, ginger, curry leaves, black pepper, and salt. Mix well.
Heat the oil for deep frying to about 175-180C (350F).

Wet your hands with water. Take a small portion of batter (about 2 tablespoons), place it on your wet palm, and flatten into a disc about 1cm thick. Poke a hole through the centre with your wet thumb to make the traditional doughnut shape.
Gently slide the shaped vadai into the hot oil. Fry in small batches without crowding, turning once or twice, for about 3-4 minutes per batch until deep golden brown and crisp on the outside.
Drain on paper towels. Serve hot with coconut sambol, pol sambol, or a thin coconut chutney.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against hungrylankan.com, topsrilankanrecipe.com, and mylankanfoodjournal.com for soaking time and grinding technique
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 5+ independent sources; universal agreement on overnight soak and minimal water during grinding as essential technique
notes: Ulundu vadai (also spelled ulundu wade, urad dal vada) is a staple Tamil Sri Lankan breakfast and festival food, eaten especially during Pongal, Diwali, and other Hindu festivals, as well as sold at roadside stalls island-wide. The total_time_min reflects the 4-8 hour soaking period, which is non-negotiable -- undersoaked dal produces a dense, hard vadai rather than the characteristically airy, crisp result. Using minimal water during grinding is the other critical technique: a too-wet batter produces flat, oily, non-fluffy vadai. The hole in the centre is both traditional and practical -- it ensures even frying all the way through without burning the outside. Vadai that are not consumed immediately will lose their crispness; they are best eaten fresh from the oil.
